## A first look, work in progress

These maps are a first look at the data for the Bren MESM group project
[New Wave of High Seas Protections](https://bren.ucsb.edu/projects/new-wave-high-seas-protections-scoping-northern-seamount-ecosystems-under-biodiversity).
The numbers may still change. Please don't cite or circulate them yet.
:::

```{r setup}
#| code-summary: "Setup: data, colours and map helpers"
# Everything here is read from small files committed to ../data by the targets
# pipeline, so this page renders without BigQuery access. See the README for
# how they're built.

# Pixel size of the site's data (degrees). It matches the project's other
# cost layers, and the file names in ../data.
pixel_size <- 0.05

all_years <- readr::read_csv(
  "../data/ais_effort_by_pixel_0p05deg_all_years.csv.gz",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
fishing_yearly <- readr::read_csv(
  "../data/ais_fishing_activity_by_pixel_0p05deg_yearly.csv.gz",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
monthly <- readr::read_csv("../data/ais_effort_by_pixel_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
download_sizes <- readr::read_csv("../data/ais_effort_by_pixel_download_sizes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
land <- sf::st_read("../data/land_ne_50m.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
study_area <- sf::st_read("../data/small_gfw_bbox_mesm/gfwbbox_sm.shp", quiet = TRUE)

# The extent of the data: the study area box pushed out to whole degrees
map_limits <- list(lon = c(-160, -120), lat = c(39, 62))

# Colours: text and chart chrome, and a one-hue blue ramp (light = little,
# dark = a lot) for every map
ink <- list(
  primary = "#0b0b0b",
  secondary = "#52514e",
  muted = "#898781",
  grid = "#e1e0d9",
  surface = "#fcfcfb"
)
land_fill <- "#e1e0d9"
sequential_blue <- c(
  "#cde2fb", "#b7d3f6", "#9ec5f4", "#86b6ef", "#6da7ec", "#5598e7", "#3987e5",
  "#2a78d6", "#256abf", "#1c5cab", "#184f95", "#104281", "#0d366b"
)
# Categorical colours, always assigned in this order
series_colours <- c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a")

theme_site <- function() {
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      plot.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = ink$surface, colour = NA),
      panel.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = ink$surface, colour = NA),
      panel.grid.major = ggplot2::element_line(colour = ink$grid, linewidth = 0.25),
      panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      text = ggplot2::element_text(colour = ink$secondary),
      axis.text = ggplot2::element_text(colour = ink$muted),
      plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(colour = ink$primary, face = "bold"),
      plot.caption = ggplot2::element_text(colour = ink$muted, hjust = 0),
      strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(colour = ink$primary),
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left"
    )
}

theme_map <- function() {
  theme_site() +
    ggplot2::theme(
      panel.grid.major = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      axis.title = ggplot2::element_blank()
    )
}

# Hours per pixel on a log scale. Vessel activity spans about nine orders of
# magnitude, from a few minutes in empty ocean to millions of hours in port,
# so the colours run from the 5th to the 99th percentile of pixels (rounded
# out to powers of ten) and anything beyond takes the end colour; the legend
# marks the two ends with <= and >=.
colour_limits <- function(hours) {
  10^c(
    floor(log10(stats::quantile(hours, 0.05))),
    ceiling(log10(stats::quantile(hours, 0.99)))
  )
}

log_labels <- function(breaks) {
  labels <- vapply(
    breaks,
    function(b) {
      if (b >= 1000) {
        scales::label_number(accuracy = 1, scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())(b)
      } else {
        format(b, scientific = FALSE, drop0trailing = TRUE, trim = TRUE)
      }
    },
    character(1)
  )
  labels[1] <- paste("≤", labels[1])
  labels[length(labels)] <- paste("≥", labels[length(labels)])
  labels
}

fill_hours <- function(name, limits) {
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = sequential_blue,
    trans = "log10",
    limits = limits,
    breaks = 10^seq(log10(limits[1]), log10(limits[2])),
    labels = log_labels,
    oob = scales::squish,
    name = name,
    guide = ggplot2::guide_colourbar(
      title.position = "top",
      barwidth = ggplot2::unit(16, "lines"),
      barheight = ggplot2::unit(0.5, "lines")
    )
  )
}

map_pixels <- function(pixels, fill_name) {
  ggplot2::ggplot() +
    ggplot2::geom_tile(
      data = pixels,
      ggplot2::aes(x = lon_center, y = lat_center, fill = hours),
      width = pixel_size,
      height = pixel_size
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_sf(data = land, fill = land_fill, colour = NA) +
    ggplot2::geom_sf(data = study_area, fill = NA, colour = ink$secondary, linewidth = 0.3) +
    fill_hours(fill_name, limits = colour_limits(pixels$hours)) +
    ggplot2::coord_sf(xlim = map_limits$lon, ylim = map_limits$lat, expand = FALSE) +
    theme_map()
}

millions <- function(x) scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.1, scale = 1e-6, suffix = " million")(x)
percent <- function(x) scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1)(x)

total_hours <- sum(all_years$hours)
fishing_hours <- sum(all_years$hours[all_years$fishing_activity])
passenger_hours <- sum(all_years$hours[all_years$vessel_class == "passenger"])
first_month <- format(min(monthly$month), "%B %Y")
last_month <- format(max(monthly$month), "%B %Y")
```

The data here are [Global Fishing Watch](https://globalfishingwatch.org)
(GFW) AIS records for every vessel GFW could identify reliably, from
`r first_month` to `r last_month`. AIS is the tracking system ships use to
broadcast their position, and GFW turns those positions into hours of
activity, with a model estimate of when fishing vessels are actually fishing.
Over the whole period there are `r millions(total_hours)` hours of vessel
activity in the area. `r millions(fishing_hours)` of them
(`r percent(fishing_hours / total_hours)`) are fishing activity.

The maps below use `r pixel_size`° pixels and the full period. The outline is
the study area box. Colours are on a log scale and capped at both ends (≤ and
≥ on the legend), so both the open ocean and the busiest lanes stay readable. The full-resolution data (0.01°, monthly, by vessel class)
is in BigQuery; see the [README](https://github.com/emlab-ucsb/mesm-gp-ne-pacific-high-seas-mpa#readme)
for what's in it and how to get it.

## Where vessels go

```{r map-all-vessels}
#| fig-cap: "Hours of activity by all vessels, January 2015 to August 2026."
all_vessels <- all_years |>
  dplyr::group_by(lon_center, lat_center) |>
  dplyr::summarise(hours = sum(hours), .groups = "drop")

map_pixels(all_vessels, "Vessel hours per pixel, all vessels")
```

Most of this is not fishing. Passenger vessels alone are
`r percent(passenger_hours / total_hours)` of all hours, and shipping lanes
and coastal traffic dominate the picture. If the cost layer is meant to
capture fishing pressure, the fishing activity map below is the better
starting point.

## Where fishing happens

```{r map-fishing}
#| fig-cap: "Hours of fishing activity, January 2015 to August 2026: fishing vessels at positions GFW's model scores as fishing."
fishing <- all_years |>
  dplyr::filter(fishing_activity) |>
  dplyr::group_by(lon_center, lat_center) |>
  dplyr::summarise(hours = sum(hours), .groups = "drop")

map_pixels(fishing, "Fishing hours per pixel")
```

### Year by year

```{r map-fishing-by-year}
#| fig-cap: "Hours of fishing activity per year. 2026 covers January to August only."
#| fig-height: 9
fishing_by_year <- fishing_yearly |>
  dplyr::group_by(year, lon_center, lat_center) |>
  dplyr::summarise(hours = sum(hours), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    year_label = dplyr::if_else(year == max(year), paste(year, "(Jan to Aug)"), as.character(year))
  )

map_pixels(fishing_by_year, "Fishing hours per pixel") +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(year_label), ncol = 4) +
  ggplot2::theme(axis.text = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

## Over time

```{r monthly-hours}
#| fig-cap: "Hours of vessel activity per month."
#| fig-height: 4.5
group_levels <- c("Passenger vessels", "Fishing vessels", "All other vessels")
monthly_groups <- monthly |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    group = dplyr::case_when(
      vessel_class == "passenger" ~ group_levels[1],
      fishing_vessel ~ group_levels[2],
      TRUE ~ group_levels[3]
    ),
    group = factor(group, levels = group_levels)
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(month, group) |>
  dplyr::summarise(hours = sum(hours), .groups = "drop")

line_ends <- monthly_groups |>
  dplyr::filter(month == max(month))

ggplot2::ggplot(monthly_groups, ggplot2::aes(x = month, y = hours, colour = group)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(
    data = line_ends,
    ggplot2::aes(label = group),
    colour = ink$secondary,
    hjust = 0,
    nudge_x = 60,
    size = 3.3
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = stats::setNames(series_colours, group_levels), name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_date(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.2))) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale()),
    limits = c(0, NA)
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Vessel hours per month") +
  theme_site()
```

Two things drive these lines: real changes in activity, and changes in how
well AIS is picked up. Satellite AIS reception has improved a lot since 2015,
so some of any rise is better coverage rather than more vessels.

```{r yearly-fishing}
#| fig-cap: "Hours of fishing activity per year. 2026 covers January to August only."
#| fig-height: 4
yearly_fishing <- fishing_yearly |>
  dplyr::group_by(year) |>
  dplyr::summarise(hours = sum(hours), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    year_label = dplyr::if_else(year == max(year), paste0(year, "\n(Jan to Aug)"), as.character(year))
  )

ggplot2::ggplot(yearly_fishing, ggplot2::aes(x = year_label, y = hours)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(fill = series_colours[1], width = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale()),
    expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Fishing hours per year") +
  theme_site() +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.major.x = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

## Getting the data

The full table is big, so aggregate it in BigQuery before you download it.
This is roughly how big a CSV would be at a few resolutions, time steps and
filters. Every cut keeps the vessel class and the two fishing columns.
Gzipping a CSV makes it about four times smaller.

```{r download-sizes}
format_size <- function(mb) {
  dplyr::if_else(
    mb >= 1000,
    paste(scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.1)(mb / 1000), "GB"),
    paste(scales::label_number(accuracy = 1)(pmax(mb, 1)), "MB")
  )
}

download_sizes |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Cut = cut,
    Rows = scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.1, scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())(n_rows),
    `CSV size` = format_size(csv_mb)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(align = c("l", "r", "r"))
```

The [README](https://github.com/emlab-ucsb/mesm-gp-ne-pacific-high-seas-mpa#readme)
has example R code for querying and downloading the table, what was filtered
out and why, and the caveats to keep in mind.

## Code, data and use of generative AI

All code is written in R and SQL and is in the [GitHub
repository](https://github.com/emlab-ucsb/mesm-gp-ne-pacific-high-seas-mpa).
The pipeline runs in BigQuery, and every number on this page is computed from
its outputs when the page is built.

Claude (Anthropic), model Opus 5.5, was used as a coding assistant through
Claude Code in October 2026. It drafted and edited the R pipeline, the SQL
queries, this page and the README. I set the study area, time window and
pixel size, chose the vessel filters and classification rules, and reviewed
the code. The model is not an author and holds no accountability: I am
responsible for all code, analysis, and conclusions here. No data, results,
or citations were produced by Claude itself. Commits made with AI assistance
carry a `Co-Authored-By: Claude` trailer, so the contribution can be
inspected commit by commit.
